item.title: Sea-level contribution from Thwaites Glacier doubles in an observation-constrained ice-sheet model
item.dc:creator: Mattia Poinelli, Eric J. Rignot, Helene L. Seroussi, Joshua Cuzzone, Tyler Pelle, Eric Larour
item.description:
Nature Communications — matched: ice sheet, grounding line, glacier, Antarctic, mass loss, sea level, sea-level rise
Abstract Thwaites Glacier is a major contributor to Antarctic mass loss and a key source of uncertainty in future sea-level rise. Ocean-driven melting at its grounding line drives rapid retreat, yet most models treat the transition between grounded and floating ice as a sharp boundary, neglecting kilometer-scale seawater intrusions that develop as the grounding line migrates and forms a grounding zone. Here, we show that actively-melting grounding zones are required to reproduce nearly three decades of observed retreat, thinning, and acceleration of Thwaites Glacier in a calibrated ice-sheet model, with successful reconstruction occurring only when grounding zones are represented as 2-5 km wide regions. Extending this model forward, we show that grounding-zone processes govern glacier’s detachment from stabilizing seafloor ridges, enabling unpinning as early as 2038 and producing up to 30 ± 6 mm of global mean sea-level rise by 2100 - approximately double previous projections even without additional climate warming.

item.title: Assessment of an updated polar stratospheric cloud parameterisation for the UK Earth System Model (UKESM1.1) within the UK Met Office Unified Model (v13.9) using CALIOP and MLS observations
item.dc:creator: Isabelle Sangha, Nathan L. Abraham, Andrew Orr, Hua Lu, Michael C. Pitts, Lamont R. Poole, … (+1)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: polar, Earth system model, Earth system, parameterization
The UK Earth System Model is updated with an improved polar stratospheric cloud scheme. The performance of the scheme is evaluated against satellite data. While the model fails to form the full range of observed ice, the scheme improves its ability to represent different polar stratospheric cloud types and their variations. This brings the model closer to satellite observations and highlights the need for further development to capture the polar stratospheric clouds with high number densities.

item.title: Subseasonal forecast improvements from sea ice concentration data assimilation in the Antarctic
item.dc:creator: Yong-Fei Zhang, Mitchell Bushuk, Michael Winton, William Gregory, Bill Hurlin, Liwei Jia, … (+1)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: Antarctic, sea ice, data assimilation
Antarctic sea ice has shifted from its overall increasing trend in the past decades to the recent decline, which attracted attention from the research community. Providing more accurate subseasonal predictions of Antarctic sea ice is critical to managing the accelerating human activities. We demonstrate that by incorporating satellite observations of sea ice concentration with modeling, the subseasonal predictions of Antarctic sea ice can be improved significantly.

item.title: Hydrological responses to climate change in a central Himalayan basin: insights from snow and glacier runoff modelling
item.dc:creator: Nirmal Kumar, Amit Kumar Dubey, Sudhir Kumar Singh, Ram L. Ray, Rupendra Prakash Singh
item.category: International Journal of River Basin Management
item.description:
International Journal of River Basin Management — matched: glacier, CMIP, climate change, SSP, emission scenario
Assessment of the impacts of climate change on central Himalayan hydrology is vital for the sustainable management of downstream water resources under recent CMIP6 climate projections. We focused on the hydrological processes and water components of the Ghaghara River basin (GRB), particularly on snow- and glacier-melt runoff under projected CMIP6 scenarios. The Spatial Processes in Hydrology (SPHY) model was calibrated and validated for the baseline period (2001–2010), achieving good-to-excellent performance at daily and monthly scales. In the baseline scenario, snow and glacier melt contributed 13.17% and 6.09% of total runoff, respectively. The snowmelt runoff declined by up to 5.49%; however, glacier melt increased by up to 6.13% under the high-emission scenario (SSP5-8.5) compared to the baseline. Rainfall-runoff is expected to increase by ~8% relative to the baseline period. Snowmelt runoff anomalies are expected to decrease after mid-century, particularly under high-emission scenarios, due to reduced snow cover during melt periods. The findings suggest that incorporating climate projections and their associated uncertainties is important for regional water management and planning.

item.title: Climatic heterogeneity determines the distribution and resilience of Tibetan Plateau rock glaciers
item.dc:creator: Xiaowen Wang, Jiaxin Cai, Lin Liu, Tingting Wu, Kai Cui, Zhiwei Zhou, … (+2)
item.description:
CATENA — matched: glacier, permafrost
Rock glaciers (RGs) are pivotal indicators of mountain permafrost, yet the environmental controls governing their distribution patterns remain poorly understood. Using a generalized boosted model and an inventory of over 40,000 RGs, this study reveals regional shifts in the dominant environmental controls of RG distribution across the Tibetan Plateau. In the westerly-dominated northwest, snow duration days are the primary control, indicating snow as the main ice source; whereas wind speed, overlooked in earlier studies, emerges as the leading driver in the monsoon-influenced southeast. Specifically, wind speeds exceeding 3.2 m·s −1 favor RG occurrence, possibly by enhancing ventilation-induced cooling within coarse blocky layers. Subregional models outperform plateau-wide models by better capturing localized environmental thresholds, underscoring the importance of regionalized approaches for permafrost prediction. Projections further suggest that climatic suitability for RG occurrence remains relatively resilient to future warming scenarios, with implications for the potential role of RGs as hydrological buffers in high-mountain environments.

item.title: Review of the Salpausselkä ice‐marginal formations in Finland
item.dc:creator: Jukka‐Pekka Palmu, Jussi Hovikoski, Reijo Pitkäranta, Antti E.K. Ojala
item.description:
Journal of Quaternary Science — matched: meltwater, deglaciation
ABSTRACT Extensive Salpausselkä ice‐marginal formations were deposited in southern and eastern Finland during the Weichselian deglaciation. These comprise three major ridges (I, II, and III Salpausselkäs) and their eastern counterparts (Tuupovaara, Koitere, and Pielisjärvi), together forming laterally continuous ice‐marginal formations extending approximately 650 km, with a total mapped length of 1530 km. Among the largest ice‐marginal deposits globally, the Salpausselkäs consist mainly of glaciofluvial sand and gravel, locally interbedded with till. They include ice‐contact deltas, subaqueous fans, sandurs, moraine slabs and ridges, and shoreline deposits, with depositional architecture strongly controlled by ice‐lobe dynamics, meltwater discharge, proglacial water depth, and bedrock topography. In this review, we synthesize the current understanding of the chronology, composition, and depositional environments of the Salpausselkäs, drawing together a substantial body of literature accumulated over the decades, including numerous studies published only in the Finnish language. Uncertainties related to their deposition, as well as topics requiring further investigation, are also discussed.

item.dc:creator: Christopher Ulloa, Ayon García, Anouk Beniest
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: glacier, permafrost
In arid zones, water comes mainly from snow, glaciers and ice-rich permafrost landforms. We introduce the Normalized Cryospheric Index (NCI), which combines ice storage and snow permanence to rank sub-watersheds where no regulatory framework exists. Applied to the Copiapó basin (Atacama, Chile), the NCI identifies the Montosa, Del Potro, Manflas and Estero Come Caballos sub-watersheds as priority targets for sustaining runoff in Chile's national water resources strategy.

item.title: Analysis of Snow Cover Dynamics in the Beas River Basin during 2019-2021
item.dc:creator: Sunita Sunita
item.description:
International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research — matched: cryosphere, climate change
Snow is a key component of the Himalayan cryosphere and plays a significant role in water resource availability and hydrological processes. This study examines the characteristics of snow cover in the Beas River Basin using MODIS satellite imagery for the period 2019-2021, with particular emphasis on temporal variations in snow cover and its potential influence on the hydrological cycle. Snow Cover Area (SCA) was estimated for the basin using the improved 8-day snow-cover product (Version 6), Terra-Aqua (MOYDGL06), generated from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) sensor. In addition, snow-cover maps were developed from the MODIS observations to analyse the spatial distribution and temporal variability of snow cover across the Beas River Basin. During the study period, SCA in the region varied from 41% (November 2020) to 90% (February 2019). SCA and total precipitation showed declining trends at rates of 2.1 km² and 47.3 cm, respectively, while the average temperature increased from 2019 to 2021 at a rate of 0.14°C. However, during 2019-2021, SCA declined at a higher rate of 19.21 km² and total precipitation decreased at a rate of 28.6 cm. In contrast, the mean temperature increased at a higher rate of 0.40°C. The study indicates that SCA and precipitation declined more rapidly during 2019-2021. The findings suggest that climate change may be an important factor influencing the observed trends in SCA, precipitation, and mean temperature. The observed SCA trend was also found to be consistent with the climatic parameters. The study examines SCA variability from January to December.

item.title: Threat and action under strain: Risk Perception Shapes Heat Protective Behavior in the Context of Differing Physical and Mental Health
item.dc:creator: Jonatan Elias Matthies, F. Junne, C. Nikendei, H.C. Friederich, K. Geue, N. Gebhardt, … (+1)
item.description:
Journal of Environmental Psychology — matched: heat wave
Heat can adversely affect both mental and physical health and increase mortality risk. Heat-related deaths are an increasing global phenomenon, particularly during heat waves or sudden temperature increases, before acclimatization can take place. For effective prevention, it is important to identify predictors of heat protection intentions and behaviors. To address the often-neglected risk that heat poses to mental health, we have developed a multidimensional questionnaire to measure heat-related risk perception. It assesses negative affect caused by heat, perceived probability of being affected by heat, and expected consequences of unprotected heat exposure. We examined the scale's relationship with heat protection intention and behavior, as well as whether mental or physical strain negatively moderated this relationship. Self-efficacy and health literacy were additional exogenous variables. A total of 1,803 adults in Germany participated in the study. The data were evaluated using structural equation modeling. After minor adjustments, the measurement model showed a fair fit. All factors of heat-related risk perception, self-efficacy, and the intention to protect oneself from heat were significantly related to heat protection behavior. Negative moderation by physical or mental strain was not detected. The results suggest that the affective factor of heat-related risk perception (e.g., “I feel afraid when I think about heat”), the intention to protect oneself, and self-efficacy are particularly decisive in determining whether people take protective measures against heat. Communication strategies that increase the emotional salience of heat hazards, which are supplemented by programs that specifically strengthen self-efficacy, could effectively elicit behavioral change in physically and mentally inconspicuous and strained populations.

item.title: Heterogeneous effects of climate change on real GDP per capita: evidence from selected MENA countries and Türkiye
item.dc:creator: Hüseyin Yılmaz
item.description:
Frontiers in Environmental Science — matched: climate change
The Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region is highly exposed to climate risks, but the economies considered in this study differ substantially in their resource structures and sectoral composition. It therefore remains unclear whether a single regional panel average can adequately reflect the relationship between climate change and real gross domestic product (GDP) per capita across these countries. This study examines this relationship using an 11-country panel covering selected MENA countries and Türkiye over the period 1995–2024, with particular attention to Gulf-non-Gulf and country-level variation. The climate variables were the temperature anomaly, the squared temperature anomaly, and the Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), with real GDP per capita as the dependent variable. The Cross-Sectionally Augmented Autoregressive Distributed Lag (CS-ARDL) model was employed as the baseline estimator to account for cross-sectional dependence and slope heterogeneity, with Common Correlated Effects Mean Group (CCEMG) and Driscoll-Kraay estimates used as complementary checks. Full-panel results show no strong and consistent average relationship between the climate variables and real GDP per capita across estimators. Subsample estimates suggest a possible negative temperature pattern in the non-Gulf group, but the corresponding marginal effects are not statistically significant at the 5% level and the pattern is not reproduced in additional sensitivity checks. Formal tests do not indicate a statistically significant difference between Gulf and non-Gulf temperature responses. Additional full-panel robustness specifications do not materially alter this conclusion. The study contributes by examining the relationship at the full-panel, subgroup, and country levels. The results suggest that regional averages may conceal some variation across countries and groups, although the small subgroup sizes limit inference and these patterns require confirmation in larger samples. Policy assessment in the region should therefore take country-level conditions into account rather than rely on a single regional average. The findings are also relevant to the broader objectives of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 8 and SDG 13.

item.title: Glacier response to the transition from lake- to land-terminating following a glacial lake outburst flood at Jinwu Glacier, southeastern Tibet
item.dc:creator: Yunyi Luo, Qiao Liu, Yin Fu, Xueyuan Lu, Yongsheng Yin, Jiawei Yang, … (+2)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: glacier
After a glacial lake outburst flood in 2020, Jinwu Glacier in southeastern Tibet lost contact with its lake. Using satellite images, we found that the glacier front slowed by about 44% and showed ice-cliff collapse and a short-lived advance. The study shows that sudden lake drainage can rapidly change glacier behaviour, with implications for how lake-terminating glaciers evolve after outburst floods.

item.title: Shifting climate in Caribbean tropical forests: Long-term trends at La Selva (Costa Rica) and El Verde (Puerto Rico)
item.dc:creator: Alonso Ramírez, Marcelo Ardón, Pavel García, Nicholas S. Marzolf, David Genereux
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: extreme event, climate change
by Alonso Ramírez, Marcelo Ardón, Pavel García, Nicholas S. Marzolf, David Genereux Climate change is altering ecosystems worldwide, but long-term, site-level hydroclimatic responses remain comparatively under-documented in many tropical regions. We analyzed long-term air and water temperature, precipitation, and stream water level data from two active Caribbean research sites: La Selva Research Station, Costa Rica, and El Verde Field Station, Puerto Rico. Our goal was to assess long-term hydroclimatic trends and changes in extreme events using continuous monitoring from automatic and manual sensors. Long-term records show a mean daily temperature of 25.1°C (1992–2024, range: 19.5-29.6°C) at La Selva and 23.6°C (2000–2024, range: 17.7-28.2°C) at El Verde. Mean annual precipitation is 4166 mm at La Selva (1983–2024) and 3635.8 mm at El Verde (1975–2024). We found a decadal warming trend of 0.29°C at both locations. The El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) influenced air temperature at El Verde, where La Niña (+0.02°C day −1 , 95% CI: 0.002–0.042) phase was associated with higher daily temperatures, but had no detectable effect on air temperature at La Selva. A significant increase in the frequency of extreme temperature events (defined as exceeding the 95 th , 97 th , and 99 th percentiles) was observed at both sites. Using the 95 th percentile and a fitted generalized linear model, both locations had ~8 extreme temperature events per year in the beginning and increased to ~35 events per year in 2024. Changes in precipitation extremes were site-specific and differed between wet and dry metrics. La Selva showed an increase in wet extremes (heavy precipitation), with 99 th percentile rainfall exceedances rising from ~1 event per year (1983–1985) to 6 per year in 2024. In contrast, El Verde showed no significant increase in heavy-precipitation events, but exhibited an increase in dry extremes (dry days th percentile at La Selva and 95 th percentile at El Verde), with estimated durations above these extreme thresholds roughly doubling over the study period. Overall, our study shows an increasing frequency of extreme events, both wet and dry, at these two Caribbean protected locations. These findings suggest important and distinct regional changes in climate over the region, with important consequences for ecosystem conservation and management.

item.title: Extensive glacier loss in the coterminous United States
item.dc:creator: Andrew G. Fountain, Bryce Glenn, Christopher J. Mcneil, Brian Menounos
item.category: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences — matched: glacier
Glaciers populate the mountain ranges of the western conterminous United States and despite their importance to alpine hydrology, their area and volume change have never been comprehensively evaluated. Our study shows that since the mid-twentieth century about one-quarter of the glaciers have disappeared and the overall area and volume are reduced by one-third. The pattern of glacier shrinkage suggests most glaciers in the conterminous United States are largely maintained by local topographic influences due to their small size. These results improve our understanding of evolving high alpine hydrology and importance to ecosystem processes.

item.title: Glacier change at the ISM-MLW transition: multi-decadal evidence of spatial heterogeneity from the Sara Umga watershed, western Himalaya
item.dc:creator: Soumik Das, Soumik Das, Suresh Das, Suresh Das, Sandip Tanu Mandal, Elora Chakraborty, … (+4)
item.description:
Frontiers in Earth Science — matched: glacier
This study presents a multi-decadal assessment of glacier change in the Sara Umga Watershed (SUW), between the Parvati and Chandra basins. The region receives a majority of its annual precipitation from Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) and a comparatively lower share contributed by winter Mid Latitude Westerlies (MLW). Using multi-temporal satellite data, we quantify changes in glacier length, area, surface velocity, elevation, debris cover, ice cliff dynamics, and high-faltitude lakes, supplemented by long-term climate trend analysis. A total of 54 glaciers (>0.05 km 2 ) were mapped, covering 128.38 ± 2.98 km 2 in 2024, of which 24.84 ± 1.15 km 2 comprised debris-covered ice. Between 1994 and 2024, total glacier area declined by 4.54 ± 0.04 km 2 (0.15 ± 0.001 km 2 yr −1 ), while debris cover expanded to 24.84 ± 1.15 km 2 (0.37 ± 0.09 km 2 yr −1 ). Frontal retreat rates for the five major glaciers ranged from ∼12 to 26.2 m yr −1 . The largest glacier, Sara Umga (GL01), exhibited a mean surface velocity of ∼23.4 m yr −1 . Elevation-change analysis reveals pronounced spatial heterogeneity in glacier thinning, with maximum surface lowering concentrated in the lower, debris-covered ablation zone (3900–4400 m a.s.l.; −1.22 ± 0.95 to −1.67 ± 0.39 m yr −1 , locally exceeding −3.0 m yr −1 ), diminishing thinning at mid-elevations, and near-equilibrium conditions across the accumulation area of GL01 (−0.07 ± 0.54 to 0.06 ± 0.33 m yr −1 ). Zones of higher thinning and flow attenuation coincide with dense ice-cliff and lake development, indicating strong melt-dynamics coupling. Climate analysis (1901–2024) shows significant winter warming (0.01 °C yr −1 ) and declining Mid-Latitude Westerly (MLW) dominated winter precipitation (−0.160 mm yr −1 ), alongside increasing pre- (0.354 mm yr −1 ) and post-monsoon (0.070 mm yr −1 ) precipitation. These findings demonstrate that changes in debris-covered Himalayan glaciers cannot be inferred from frontal retreat alone. Instead, coupled changes in thickness, velocity, surface morphology, and climate trends govern long-term glacier response and hence should be studied alongside.

item.title: Study of Snow Cover Characteristics According to the Data of Meteorological Stations of Western Kazakhstan in the Context of Global Climate Change
item.dc:creator: Akhmetkal Rakhmetullayevich Medeu, V. V. Zhdanov, Viktor Blagovechshenskiy, Nina V. Pimankina
item.description:
Water — matched: climate change
In the Republic of Kazakhstan, runoff in lowland rivers is 90% determined by snowmelt. Therefore, assessing snow reserves in a changing climate is of great scientific and applied importance. This work aims to assess how global climate change affects snow cover characteristics in Western Kazakhstan in the Caspian Sea basin. For the first time, we conducted a comprehensive assessment of snow cover depth, water equivalent, and snow cover duration in the drainage basin. We used statistical analysis of data from 50 meteorological stations for the period 1950–2024. Only data from 14 meteorological stations in the Mugalzhar lowlands (north of the Aktobe region) and on the Podural plateau (north of the West Kazakhstan region), where errors did not exceed 2–4%, were suitable for climate studies. The results showed an increase in average snow height by 3 cm, a decrease in maximum height by 4 cm, and a 17-day reduction in the duration of stable snow cover. However, these trends are not statistically significant (the coefficient of determination is 0.02–0.24), and their values fall within the statistical error. The calculated Pearson and Spearman indicators confirm a statistical relationship between individual global and regional climate indicators (correlation coefficients of 0.23–0.40 at the significance level p = 0.03). However, most snow cover indicators show no statistical dependence: correlation coefficients range from −0.02 to 0.20, with p = 0.30–0.90. The results obtained indicate a random, stochastic nature of the long-term dynamics of depth, water equivalent, and duration of snow cover in the region under study.

item.title: Past moisture and vegetation conditions at Lake Aura, Norway using n -alkanes and pollen
item.dc:creator: Anastasia Bertheussen, David Keith Wright, Jago Jonathan Birk, Calin Constantin Steindal, Sabine Fiedler, Stefanie Klassen, … (+2)
item.description:
The Holocene — matched: Holocene, proxy
Wetlands are valuable paleoenvironmental archives where pollen and n -alkane samples can be collected and used to reconstruct local vegetation patterns and hydrological conditions. However, the impact of local environmental heterogeneity on n -alkanes specifically remains poorly constrained. To address this, we apply a combined n -alkane and pollen approach which allows for a more nuanced reconstruction. In this study, we analyze three separate peat cores around Lake Aura, a high-altitude lake in central Norway, to reconstruct the Holocene vegetation and hydrological development. The area has extensive evidence of successive archaeological activity, and human impacts on vegetation are considered. Our records show a general pattern of arboreal dominance, but with increasing percentages of grassy vegetation towards the Late Holocene, possibly associated with the onset and intensification of pastoralism. Although pollen and n -alkane records broadly converge, intervals where the n -alkane wood/grass ratio rises while the arboreal pollen declines show that the proxies capture different aspects of vegetation change, refining the overall reconstruction. Our study demonstrates the value of combining pollen with molecular markers for reconstructing Holocene vegetation and moisture patterns, and we highlight the broader potential of this tandem approach for refining paleoenvironmental reconstructions in heterogeneous landscapes.

item.title: High-performance geodynamics on GPUs using the PETSc CUDA backend (GAUZZ v1.0.0)

item.title: Physics vs. AI in weather prediction: evaluating GraphCast, AIFS, and FuXi against an observation-corrected WRF model for flash floods
item.dc:creator: Haseeb ur Rehman, Félicia Norma Rebecca Teferle
item.description:

Artificial intelligence (AI) weather models are now competing with traditional physics-based models for flood forecasting. We tested three of them and a physics-based model against observations from three flood events in Luxembourg. The AI models detected light rain and predicted temperatures better, but the physics-based model was more skilful at the heavy rainfall that actually causes floods. One AI model kept its skill on an event after its training period.
